summary.text: At \(n=67\), the two distinct integers \(147\) and \(2055\) both give residue sums equal to \(67\): for \(147\), \(1+3+3+3+19+19+19=67\), while for \(2055\), \(1+3+9\cdot7=67\). Thus \(67\) occurs at least twice, contradicting the claimed multiplicity one.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(m)=\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor \log_2 m\rfloor}(m\bmod 2^k)
\]
be the sequence A049802. Here \(m\bmod 2^k\) is the least nonnegative residue of \(m\) modulo \(2^k\). For positive \(n\), the definition used for A383327 is
\[
a(n)=\#\{m:0\le m<2^{n+1}\text{ and }F(m)=n\}.
\]
The upper bound is sufficient to contain every occurrence relevant to this count. For the disproof, however, no completeness property of the bound is needed: it is enough to exhibit two distinct integers below the bound at which \(F\) has the same claimed uniquely occurring value.

We disprove the assertion at the listed value \(n=67\). Consider the two distinct integers
\[
m_1=147\qquad\text{and}\qquad m_2=2055.
\]
We compute \(F\) at each of them directly.

First,
\[
2^7=128\le 147<256=2^8,
\]
so \(\lfloor\log_2 147\rfloor=7\). The residues of \(147\) modulo the powers \(2^k\), for \(1\le k\le7\), are as follows:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
k&2^k&147\bmod 2^k\\ \hline
1&2&1\\
2&4&3\\
3&8&3\\
4&16&3\\
5&32&19\\
6&64&19\\
7&128&19
\end{array}
\]
Indeed, these follow respectively from
\[
\begin{aligned}
147&=73\cdot2+1,\\
147&=36\cdot4+3,\\
147&=18\cdot8+3,\\
147&=9\cdot16+3,\\
147&=4\cdot32+19,\\
147&=2\cdot64+19,\\
147&=1\cdot128+19.
\end{aligned}
\]
Each displayed remainder is between \(0\) and one less than its modulus, so these are indeed the least nonnegative residues. Therefore
\[
F(147)=1+3+3+3+19+19+19=10+57=67.
\]

Next,
\[
2^{11}=2048\le2055<4096=2^{12},
\]
so \(\lfloor\log_2 2055\rfloor=11\). For the first two powers of two,
\[
2055\bmod2=1,
\qquad
2055\bmod4=3.
\]
For every \(k\) with \(3\le k\le11\), write
\[
2055=2048+7=2^{11}+7.
\]
Because \(2^k\) divides \(2^{11}\) whenever \(k\le11\), it follows that
\[
2055\equiv7\pmod{2^k}.
\]
Moreover, for \(k\ge3\), one has \(0\le7<2^k\), so the least nonnegative residue is exactly \(7\). Thus the eleven summands defining \(F(2055)\) are
\[
1,\ 3,\ \underbrace{7,7,7,7,7,7,7,7,7}_{k=3,\ldots,11}.
\]
There are nine copies of \(7\), and hence
\[
F(2055)=1+3+9\cdot7=4+63=67.
\]

Both indices occur in the finite set counted by \(a(67)\). Indeed,
\[
147<2055<4096=2^{12}<2^{68}=2^{67+1}.
\]
We have proved that both satisfy the required equation \(F(m)=67\), and they are distinct because \(147\ne2055\). Consequently,
\[
\#\{m:0\le m<2^{68}\text{ and }F(m)=67\}\ge2,
\]
so
\[
a(67)\ge2.
\]
In particular, \(a(67)\ne1\).

Finally, \(67\) is one of the numbers in the conjecture's set
\[
\{1,3,5,9,15,23,35,63,65,67\}.
\]
The conjecture asserts \(a(n)=1\) for every member of this set, and therefore in particular asserts \(a(67)=1\). The two explicit occurrences above contradict that assertion. Hence the conjecture is false.
